introduction-the-security-gatekeeper.core: Linux's basic access control is discretionary: every file has an owner user, an owner group, and permission bits for user, group and others. On every access the kernel checks the process's effective UID and GIDs against them, and root (UID 0) bypasses most checks. Special bits (setuid, setgid, sticky), umask defaults and ACLs extend the model, while LSMs (SELinux, AppArmor) add mandatory controls on top.

first_principles.problem: A web app can't write its upload directory, and a junior engineer 'fixes' it with chmod 777.
truths: Every file has an owner and group.

analogy.title: A building with keycards per floor
analogy.story: Your card opens your office, your team's shared room, and the lobby; 777 is propping every door open.
analogy.breaks: Propped doors are visible; 777 permissions silently invite abuse.

code.text:
ps -o user= -p $(pgrep -o gunicorn)     # www-data
ls -ld /srv/app/uploads                  # drwxr-xr-x root root
chown root:www-data /srv/app/uploads && chmod 2775 /srv/app/uploads
# group write + setgid so new files keep the group

check.q: Why is chmod 777 a poor fix for permission errors?
check.a: It grants every user write and execute access, violating least privilege and enabling tampering or code execution.

viewing-permissions-the-ls-l-command.core: ls -l shows a 10-character mode: the file type (- regular, d directory, l symlink, c/b device, s socket, p pipe), then three rwx triads for user, group and others, with s, S, t or T marking special bits and a trailing + indicating an ACL. Then come the link count, owner, group, size, modification time and name. stat gives octal mode, inode and all timestamps, and namei -l walks permissions along a whole path.

first_principles.problem: An engineer can't tell why access fails, because the problem is a parent directory missing x permission.
truths: Mode strings encode type and permissions.

analogy.title: Reading a door's sign panel
analogy.story: Three rows: what the owner, the team and visitors may do, plus symbols for special rules.
analogy.breaks: Door signs are per door; access also depends on every directory along the path.

code.text:
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
# -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 68208 ... /usr/bin/passwd   (s = setuid)
stat -c '%a %A %U:%G %n' /srv/data/report.csv
namei -l /srv/data/report.csv
# drwx------ alice alice data   ← parent blocks others

check.q: What does a lowercase 's' in the user execute position mean?
check.a: The setuid bit is set and the file is executable by the owner.

the-rwx-triad-read-write-execute.core: For files: r means read contents, w means modify contents, x means execute as a program. For directories, meanings differ: r means list names, w means create, delete or rename entries (with x), and x means traverse (access entries by name and cd into it). So deleting a file depends on the directory's w permission, not the file's, and a directory with x but not r lets you open known names without listing them.

first_principles.problem: A user can delete a read-only file they don't own because the directory is group-writable.
truths: Files and directories interpret bits differently.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet vs the documents in it
analogy.story: Permission to rearrange the cabinet (directory w) lets you remove a document even if you can't edit it.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets don't have traverse rights; directories need x to reach anything inside.

code.text:
mkdir box && touch box/f && chmod 111 box   # --x--x--x
ls box          # Permission denied (no r)
cat box/f       # works if f readable (x allows traversal)
chmod 755 box && chmod 444 box/f && chmod o+w box
# other users can now delete box/f despite it being read-only

check.q: What permission on a directory allows deleting a file inside it?
check.a: Write plus execute (w and x) on the directory, regardless of the file's own permissions (unless the sticky bit is set).

changing-permissions-chmod-symbolic-mode.core: Symbolic chmod modifies specific bits relative to current ones: who (u, g, o, a), operator (+ add, - remove, = set exactly), and permissions (r, w, x, X, s, t). For example chmod g+w file, chmod o-rwx secret, chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= script. X (capital) adds execute only to directories and to files already executable by someone, which makes recursive changes safe (chmod -R g+rX).

first_principles.problem: chmod -R 755 on a tree makes every data file executable.
truths: Recursive changes hit files and dirs alike.

analogy.title: Editing a guest list by adding or crossing out names
analogy.story: You adjust specific entries instead of rewriting the whole list.
analogy.breaks: Guest lists have one row; chmod has three triads plus special bits.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Group can read and traverse; files stay non-executable.

code.text:
chmod -R g+rX,o-rwx /srv/shared       # dirs traversable, files not made executable
chmod u+x deploy.sh
chmod a=r,u+w config.yaml             # 644
ls -l /srv/shared | head

check.q: What does capital X do in chmod -R g+rX?
check.a: Adds execute only for directories (and files already executable), so traversal works without making data files executable.

changing-permissions-chmod-octal-mode.core: Octal chmod sets all bits at once: each digit is the sum r=4, w=2, x=1 for user, group and others. Common modes: 644 (rw-r--r--, files), 755 (rwxr-xr-x, executables and dirs), 600 (rw-------, secrets), 700 (private dirs), 640 (group-readable configs), and 2775 (shared dir with setgid). It's precise and scriptable but replaces everything, so know the full intended mode.

first_principles.problem: An SSH private key with mode 644 is rejected with 'UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE'.

analogy.title: A three-digit combination code
analogy.story: Each digit sets the access for one group of people in one go.
analogy.breaks: Combination locks hide codes; modes are visible to everyone.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: SSH accepts the key; config readable by app group only.

code.text:
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
chmod 640 /etc/app/db.conf && chown root:app /etc/app/db.conf
stat -c '%a %n' ~/.ssh/*

check.q: What octal mode gives the owner read/write and nobody else any access?

changing-ownership-chown-and-chgrp.core: chown user:group file changes owner and group (chown user, chown :group, chown -R for trees), and chgrp group changes only the group. Only root (CAP_CHOWN) can give files away to other users, which prevents quota evasion and spoofing; owners can change a file's group to groups they belong to. Changing ownership clears setuid and setgid bits for safety. Use -h for symlinks themselves, and --reference to copy ownership.

first_principles.problem: After copying files as root, a service can't read its own data directory because everything is root-owned.
truths: Only root can give files away.

analogy.title: Transferring a car's registration
analogy.story: Only the registry (root) can put a car in someone else's name; you can't dump your car on a stranger.
analogy.breaks: Car transfers need paperwork; chown -R can silently change thousands of files.

branches.label: Rules
children: Owner can change to own groups

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Service owns its data; config readable by group.

code.text:
chown -R app:app /var/lib/app
install -d -o app -g app -m 0750 /var/lib/app/cache
install -o root -g app -m 0640 app.conf /etc/app/app.conf
find /var/lib/app ! -user app -ls | head   # verify

check.q: Why can't a normal user chown their file to another user?
check.a: To prevent evading disk quotas and spoofing ownership; giving files away requires root (CAP_CHOWN).

default-permissions-umask.core: New files start from 666 and directories from 777, and the process's umask removes bits from that. A umask of 022 gives files 644 and directories 755; 027 gives 640 and 750 (no world access); 077 gives 600 and 700. It's inherited by child processes and set in shell profiles, systemd units (UMask=) or services, and explains why files created by an app are or aren't group-writable.

first_principles.problem: Files created by a shared build service aren't group-writable, so teammates can't update them.
truths: umask is per process and inherited.

analogy.title: A stencil over a paint roller
analogy.story: The roller would paint everything; the stencil blocks the parts you don't want.
analogy.breaks: Stencils are physical; umask is invisible unless you check it.

code.text:
umask            # 0022
( umask 002; touch shared.txt; ls -l shared.txt )   # -rw-rw-r--
# /etc/systemd/system/builder.service.d/umask.conf
# [Service]
# UMask=0002

check.q: With umask 027, what permissions will a newly created file and directory get?

special-permissions-suid-set-user-id.core: The setuid bit on an executable (shown as s in the user execute slot, octal 4xxx) makes it run with the file owner's effective UID rather than the caller's. That's how passwd (owned by root) can update /etc/shadow for ordinary users. Setuid-root binaries are prime privilege-escalation targets, since any bug becomes root access, so keep them few, audit them, mount untrusted filesystems nosuid, and prefer capabilities or sudo rules.

first_principles.problem: An attacker with a shell finds a custom setuid-root backup script and escalates to root.
truths: Bugs in setuid-root code mean root.
derivation: Never setuid **scripts** (ignored by kernel, but wrappers are risky).

analogy.title: A borrowed master key for one task
analogy.story: The locksmith lends you their master key only inside a specific room, but if that room has a hidden exit, you're loose with the master key.
analogy.breaks: Borrowed keys can be returned; exploited setuid gives persistent root.

code.text:
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -l {} + 2>/dev/null
# compare against package-owned list
rpm -Vf /usr/bin/passwd 2>/dev/null || dpkg -S /usr/bin/passwd
chmod u-s /usr/local/bin/backup.sh    # remove unexpected setuid

check.q: Why is a setuid-root binary a common privilege escalation target?
check.a: It runs with root privileges for any user, so any vulnerability in it gives the attacker root.

special-permissions-sgid-set-group-id.core: setgid on an executable runs it with the file's group as the effective GID, for example to access a group-owned resource. On a directory (more common) it makes new files and subdirectories inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group, and new subdirectories also get setgid. Combined with a group-writable mode and umask 002, it creates reliable shared team directories.

first_principles.problem: Files in a team share end up owned by each user's personal group, so teammates can't edit them.
truths: New files take the creator's primary group by default.

analogy.title: A team folder that stamps every new document with the team name
analogy.story: Whoever creates a document, it automatically belongs to the team.
analogy.breaks: Stamps don't control editing; group write bits and umask still matter.

code.text:
groupadd analytics && usermod -aG analytics alice && usermod -aG analytics bob
mkdir -p /srv/analytics && chgrp analytics /srv/analytics && chmod 2775 /srv/analytics
su - alice -c 'umask 002; touch /srv/analytics/q3.csv'
ls -l /srv/analytics/q3.csv     # -rw-rw-r-- alice analytics

check.q: What does setgid on a directory do?
check.a: New files and subdirectories inherit the directory's group (and subdirectories inherit setgid), instead of the creator's primary group.

special-permissions-the-sticky-bit.core: The sticky bit on a directory (t in the others execute slot, octal 1xxx) restricts deletion and renaming. In a world-writable directory only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root can delete or rename a file. /tmp is 1777 for this reason: everyone can create files, but nobody can delete others'. Without it, any user could remove or replace other users' temporary files, which enables attacks.

first_principles.problem: In a shared upload directory, one user deletes everyone else's files.
truths: Directory write allows deleting any entry.

analogy.title: A communal notice board where you can only remove your own notices
analogy.story: Everyone can pin notices, but only the author or the board manager can take one down.
analogy.breaks: Notice boards are policed by people; sticky bits by the kernel.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Users can only delete their own uploads.

code.text:
ls -ld /tmp        # drwxrwxrwt
chmod 1777 /srv/uploads
find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 2>/dev/null   # world-writable without sticky

check.q: Why does /tmp have the sticky bit set?
check.a: So that although everyone can create files there, users can only delete or rename their own files.

combining-special-bits-the-four-digit-oc.core: A fourth leading octal digit encodes special bits: 4 is setuid, 2 setgid and 1 sticky, summed like the others. Examples: 4755 (setuid executable), 2775 (setgid shared dir), 1777 (sticky world-writable dir, /tmp) and 3775 (setgid plus sticky team dir). In ls -l, a lowercase s or t means the special bit plus execute; uppercase S or T means the special bit without execute, which is usually a mistake.

first_principles.problem: A shared directory shows drwxrwSr-x and new files aren't working as expected.
truths: Special bits occupy a fourth digit.

analogy.title: A fourth dial on the combination lock
analogy.story: It controls special behaviours on top of the normal three access dials.
analogy.breaks: Locks don't display their combination; ls does, with tricky letter cases.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Group can traverse; setgid works as intended.

code.text:
stat -c '%a %A %n' /srv/team    # 2765 drwxrwSr-x   ← setgid without group x
chmod 2775 /srv/team
stat -c '%a %A %n' /srv/team    # 2775 drwxrwsr-x

check.q: What does mode 3775 on a directory mean?
check.a: setgid (2) + sticky (1) with rwxrwxr-x: new files inherit the group, and users can only delete their own files.

access-control-lists-acls-beyond-basic-p.core: POSIX ACLs add named entries beyond owner, group and others: user:alice:rw-, group:auditors:r-x, plus a mask limiting maximum group-class permissions, and default ACLs on directories that new files inherit. Manage them with setfacl and getfacl, and look for + in ls -l. They solve 'give one more user or group access' without restructuring groups. Keep them minimal and documented, since they're easy to overlook.

first_principles.problem: An auditor group needs read-only access to app logs owned by app:app without changing ownership.

analogy.title: Adding named guests to a guest list
analogy.story: Beyond 'owner, family, public', you write specific names with specific rights.
analogy.breaks: Guest lists are visible on the door; ACLs only show as a '+' in ls.

code.text:
setfacl -R -m g:auditors:rX /var/log/app
setfacl -d -m g:auditors:rX /var/log/app     # new logs inherit
getfacl /var/log/app | head
# group:auditors:r-x
# default:group:auditors:r-x

check.q: What does the ACL mask entry do?
check.a: Limits the maximum effective permissions for named users, named groups and the owning group.
